claim: The Drosophila Pan Gu (PNG) kinase complex regulates hundreds of maternal mRNAs that become translationally repressed or activated as the oocyte transitions to an embryo.
source: The Drosophila Pan Gu (PNG) kinase complex regulates hundreds of maternal mRNAs that become translationally repressed or activated as the oocyte transitions to an embryo.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Hara et al., 2017) and references to published data (Kronja et al., 2014) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: PNG activity is under tight developmental control and restricted to the oocyte-to-embryo transition.
source: In a previous paper (Hara et al., 2017), we demonstrated PNG activity is under tight developmental control and restricted to this transition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Hara et al., 2017).

claim: PNG is a threonine kinase.
source: PNG is a threonine kinase
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from positional scanning peptide library showing PNG preferentially phosphorylates threonine over serine.

claim: PNG lacks a clear phosphorylation site consensus sequence.
source: examination of PNG specificity showed it to be a Thr-kinase yet lacking a clear phosphorylation site consensus sequence
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from peptide library screening showing no strong consensus sequence was identified.

claim: Trailer Hitch (TRAL) is a PNG substrate.
source: An unbiased biochemical screen for PNG substrates identified the conserved translational repressor Trailer Hitch (TRAL).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the biochemical substrate screen using thio-phosphorylation and mass spectrometry.

claim: Phosphomimetic mutation of the PNG phospho-sites in TRAL reduced its ability to inhibit translation in vitro.
source: Phosphomimetic mutation of the PNG phospho-sites in TRAL reduced its ability to inhibit translation in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro translation assays using rabbit reticulocyte lysate with phosphomimetic TRAL mutants.

claim: Mutation of tral dominantly suppressed png mutants in vivo.
source: In vivo, mutation of tral dominantly suppressed png mutants and restored Cyclin B protein levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing genetic interaction between png and tral mutations.

claim: Mutation of tral restored Cyclin B protein levels in png mutants.
source: In vivo, mutation of tral dominantly suppressed png mutants and restored Cyclin B protein levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunoblot analysis of Cyclin B protein levels in mutant embryos.

claim: Pumilio (PUM) is a PNG substrate.
source: The repressor Pumilio (PUM) has the same relationship with PNG, and we also show that PUM is a PNG substrate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro kinase assays showing PNG phosphorylates PUM.

claim: PNG can phosphorylate BICC.
source: Furthermore, PNG can phosphorylate BICC and ME31B, repressors that bind TRAL in cytoplasmic RNPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro kinase assays showing PNG phosphorylates BICC.

claim: PNG can phosphorylate ME31B.
source: Furthermore, PNG can phosphorylate BICC and ME31B, repressors that bind TRAL in cytoplasmic RNPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro kinase assays showing PNG phosphorylates ME31B.

claim: PNG likely promotes translation at the oocyte-to-embryo transition by phosphorylating and inactivating translational repressors.
source: Therefore, PNG likely promotes translation at the oocyte-to-embryo transition by phosphorylating and inactivating translational repressors.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results showing PNG phosphorylates translational repressors and that phosphomimetic mutations reduce their repressive activity.

claim: Profound changes in mRNA translation accompany egg activation in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, profound changes in mRNA translation accompany egg activation, with hundreds of maternal mRNAs becoming repressed and nearly a thousand translationally activated (Kronja et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Kronja et al., 2014).

claim: Hundreds of maternal mRNAs become repressed during egg activation in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, profound changes in mRNA translation accompany egg activation, with hundreds of maternal mRNAs becoming repressed and nearly a thousand translationally activated (Kronja et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Kronja et al., 2014).

claim: Nearly a thousand maternal mRNAs become translationally activated during egg activation in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, profound changes in mRNA translation accompany egg activation, with hundreds of maternal mRNAs becoming repressed and nearly a thousand translationally activated (Kronja et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Kronja et al., 2014).

claim: Translation changes during egg activation occur in a brief window of less than an hour.
source: These translation changes occur in a brief window of less than an hour, and the majority are controlled by the PNG kinase complex (Kronja et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Kronja et al., 2014).

claim: The majority of translation changes during egg activation are controlled by the PNG kinase complex.
source: These translation changes occur in a brief window of less than an hour, and the majority are controlled by the PNG kinase complex (Kronja et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Kronja et al., 2014).

claim: The PNG kinase complex is composed of the PNG catalytic subunit, GNU, and PLU.
source: This kinase complex is composed of the PNG catalytic subunit, whose activity requires the physical association of two activating subunits, GNU and PLU (Freeman et al., 1986; Elfring et al., 1997; Fenger et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Freeman et al., 1986; Elfring et al., 1997; Fenger et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2003).

claim: PNG activity requires the physical association of GNU and PLU activating subunits.
source: This kinase complex is composed of the PNG catalytic subunit, whose activity requires the physical association of two activating subunits, GNU and PLU (Freeman et al., 1986; Elfring et al., 1997; Fenger et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Freeman et al., 1986; Elfring et al., 1997; Fenger et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2003).

claim: The activity of PNG is restricted to the window of egg activation by developmental control of GNU binding to PNG and PLU.
source: We recently demonstrated that the activity of PNG is restricted to the window of egg activation by exquisite developmental control of the binding of GNU to PNG and PLU (Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Hara et al., 2017).

claim: PNG controls both mRNAs that become repressed and those that become activated at the oocyte-to-embryo transition.
source: PNG is likely to have many targets, given that it controls both mRNAs that become repressed and those that become activated at the oocyte-to-embryo transition (Kronja et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Kronja et al., 2014).

claim: PNG promotes the translation of smg mRNA.
source: PNG promotes the translation of smg mRNA, a translational repressor that can promote deadenylation (Tadros et al., 2007; Eichhorn et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Tadros et al., 2007; Eichhorn et al., 2016).

claim: SMG is a translational repressor that can promote deadenylation.
source: PNG promotes the translation of smg mRNA, a translational repressor that can promote deadenylation (Tadros et al., 2007; Eichhorn et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Tadros et al., 2007; Eichhorn et al., 2016).

claim: Most mRNAs whose translational repression is dependent on PNG undergo SMG-dependent deadenylation.
source: Most, but not all, of the mRNAs whose translational repression is dependent on PNG undergo SMG-dependent deadenylation (Eichhorn et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Eichhorn et al., 2016).

claim: The role of PNG in translation repression can largely be explained by its effect in activating translation of smg mRNA.
source: Thus, the role of PNG in translation repression can largely be explained by its effect in activating translation of smg mRNA.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that PNG promotes smg translation and most PNG-dependent repressed mRNAs undergo SMG-dependent deadenylation.

claim: PNG exhibited a strong preference to phosphorylate threonine over serine.
source: PNG exhibited a strong preference to phosphorylate threonine, because peptides whose phospho-acceptor site (position 0) was fixed with threonine were strongly phosphorylated, whereas serine peptides were phosphorylated at reduced levels (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from positional scanning peptide library shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: PNG was most strongly selective for hydrophobic amino acids at −3 relative to the phosphorylated residue.
source: Although no strong consensus sequence was identified, PNG was most strongly selective for hydrophobic amino acids at −3 relative to the phosphorylated residue, and it had some preferences for aromatic residues at position −2 and for arginine at position +2 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from positional scanning peptide library shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PNG had some preferences for aromatic residues at position −2 relative to the phosphorylated residue.
source: Although no strong consensus sequence was identified, PNG was most strongly selective for hydrophobic amino acids at −3 relative to the phosphorylated residue, and it had some preferences for aromatic residues at position −2 and for arginine at position +2 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from positional scanning peptide library shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PNG had some preferences for arginine at position +2 relative to the phosphorylated residue.
source: Although no strong consensus sequence was identified, PNG was most strongly selective for hydrophobic amino acids at −3 relative to the phosphorylated residue, and it had some preferences for aromatic residues at position −2 and for arginine at position +2 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from positional scanning peptide library shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Kinases with a preference for threonine over serine are atypical.
source: Kinases with a preference for threonine over serine are atypical, and this specificity is conferred by a beta-branched amino acid residue immediately downstream of the conserved DFG sequence in the kinase activation loop (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Chen et al., 2014).

claim: Threonine specificity in kinases is conferred by a beta-branched amino acid residue immediately downstream of the conserved DFG sequence in the kinase activation loop.
source: Kinases with a preference for threonine over serine are atypical, and this specificity is conferred by a beta-branched amino acid residue immediately downstream of the conserved DFG sequence in the kinase activation loop (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Chen et al., 2014).

claim: In PNG, the amino acid corresponding to the position immediately downstream of the DFG sequence is an isoleucine.
source: In PNG, the corresponding amino acid is an isoleucine, which would be predicted to produce a threonine preference (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The isoleucine at position 87 in PNG would be predicted to produce a threonine preference.
source: In PNG, the corresponding amino acid is an isoleucine, which would be predicted to produce a threonine preference (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from established knowledge about kinase specificity determinants and the sequence of PNG.

claim: Endogenous kinases in embryonic extracts were inactivated by treatment with FSBA.
source: The endogenous kinases in the extracts from early embryos were inactivated by treatment with 5'-(4-fluorosulphonylbenzoyl)adenosine (FSBA), which covalently binds to kinases at a conserved lysine in the ATP hydrolysis site (Knight et al., 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and citation to published work (Knight et al., 2012).

claim: FSBA covalently binds to kinases at a conserved lysine in the ATP hydrolysis site.
source: The endogenous kinases in the extracts from early embryos were inactivated by treatment with 5'-(4-fluorosulphonylbenzoyl)adenosine (FSBA), which covalently binds to kinases at a conserved lysine in the ATP hydrolysis site (Knight et al., 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Knight et al., 2012).

claim: Phosphorylation occurred with wild-type PNG but not the kinase-dead form in embryonic extracts.
source: Western blot analysis with an antibody against alkylated-thio-phosphate (Allen et al., 2007) showed that endogenous kinases in the extract had been inactivated, and phosphorylation occurred with wild-type PNG but not the kinase-dead form (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 45 proteins were phosphorylated by wild-type PNG kinase in the pilot substrate screen.
source: A pilot screen was done with wild-type PNG kinase and 45 proteins were phosphorylated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the pilot substrate screen.

claim: 27 proteins identified in the pilot experiment were also identified in the second substrate screen.
source: These included 27 of the proteins identified in the pilot experiment (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: A high representation of phosphopeptides was recovered for TRAL with wild-type but not kinase-dead PNG.
source: A high representation of phosphopeptides was recovered for the translational repressor Trailer Hitch (TRAL) with wild-type but not kinase-dead PNG (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 19 out of 36 PNG substrates identified were proteins known to be involved in mRNA translation.
source: Out of 36 substrates identified, 19 were proteins known to be involved in mRNA translation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the substrate screen and knowledge of protein functions.

claim: The recovery of substrates was not due solely to the abundance of the proteins in the extracts.
source: Note that the recovery of substrates was not due solely to the abundance of the proteins in the extracts (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: 79% of the identified unique peptides had threonine as the phospho-acceptor residue.
source: 79% of the identified unique peptides had threonine as the phospho-acceptor residue (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The identified peptides showed an enrichment of hydrophobic residues at −3 position.
source: The identified peptides showed an enrichment of hydrophobic residues at −3 position as in the peptide library, confirming that PNG tends to phosphorylate threonine three residues downstream of a hydrophobic amino acid (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The threonine preference was highly significant in the context of the Drosophila proteome.
source: The threonine preference was also highly significant (log-odds value of 80.5) in the context of the Drosophila proteome (O'Shea et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and citation to published work (O'Shea et al., 2013).

claim: 15 amino acids in TRAL were phosphorylated by PNG in embryonic extracts.
source: 15 amino acids (13 of them threonine), clustered in the C-terminal half of the protein, were phosphorylated by PNG in embryonic extracts (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 13 of the 15 PNG phosphorylation sites in TRAL are threonine residues.
source: 15 amino acids (13 of them threonine), clustered in the C-terminal half of the protein, were phosphorylated by PNG in embryonic extracts (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PNG phosphorylation sites in TRAL are clustered in the C-terminal half of the protein.
source: 15 amino acids (13 of them threonine), clustered in the C-terminal half of the protein, were phosphorylated by PNG in embryonic extracts (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The full-length TRAL protein was phosphorylated by PNG in vitro.
source: The full-length protein and the C-terminal half, but not the N-terminal half, were phosphorylated by PNG in vitro (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The C-terminal half of TRAL was phosphorylated by PNG in vitro.
source: The full-length protein and the C-terminal half, but not the N-terminal half, were phosphorylated by PNG in vitro (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The N-terminal half of TRAL was not phosphorylated by PNG in vitro.
source: The full-length protein and the C-terminal half, but not the N-terminal half, were phosphorylated by PNG in vitro (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Substitution of all 15 PNG phosphorylation sites in TRAL to alanine reduced phosphorylation by PNG.
source: For both the full-length protein and the C-terminal half, the level of phosphorylation by PNG was reduced with the alanine-substituted forms (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There may be other potential PNG phosphorylation sites in the C-terminus of TRAL that were not detected in the screen.
source: Residual phosphorylation of the alanine-substituted form of TRAL raises the possibility that there are other potential PNG phosphorylation sites in the C-terminus of TRAL that were not detected in the screen.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation of residual phosphorylation in the alanine-substituted TRAL mutant.

claim: TRAL is a member of the (L)Sm protein family.
source: TRAL is a member of the (L)Sm protein family composed of RAP55 in vertebrates, CAR1 in C. elegans, and Sdc6 in yeast (Wilhelm et al., 2005; Marnef et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Wilhelm et al., 2005; Marnef et al., 2009).

claim: RAP55 from Xenopus is able to inhibit translation in vitro.
source: RAP55 from Xenopus and Sdc6 from yeast are able to inhibit translation in vitro (Tanaka et al., 2006; Nissan et al., 2010), in yeast apparently by blocking the function of the eIF4G subunit of the eIF4F initiation factor (Rajyaguru et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Tanaka et al., 2006; Nissan et al., 2010).

claim: Sdc6 from yeast is able to inhibit translation in vitro.
source: RAP55 from Xenopus and Sdc6 from yeast are able to inhibit translation in vitro (Tanaka et al., 2006; Nissan et al., 2010), in yeast apparently by blocking the function of the eIF4G subunit of the eIF4F initiation factor (Rajyaguru et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Tanaka et al., 2006; Nissan et al., 2010).

claim: Sdc6 inhibits translation in yeast by blocking the function of the eIF4G subunit of the eIF4F initiation factor.
source: RAP55 from Xenopus and Sdc6 from yeast are able to inhibit translation in vitro (Tanaka et al., 2006; Nissan et al., 2010), in yeast apparently by blocking the function of the eIF4G subunit of the eIF4F initiation factor (Rajyaguru et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Rajyaguru et al., 2012).

claim: Drosophila TRAL inhibited translation of GFP-Myc mRNA in reticulocyte lysates.
source: We examined translation of an mRNA encoding Myc-tagged GFP in reticulocyte lysates and found that as for other family members, addition of Drosophila TRAL inhibited translation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro translation assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The phosphomimetic form of TRAL suppressed translational repression.
source: Strikingly, the phosphomimetic mutations suppressed the translational repression by TRAL (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro translation assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: TRAL with alanine substitutions at the PNG phosphorylation sites still inhibited translation of the reporter mRNA.
source: In contrast, TRAL in which these residues were replaced by alanine still inhibited translation of the reporter mRNA in the extracts (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro translation assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Phosphorylation of TRAL by PNG is consistent with relieving its ability to repress translation.
source: These results are consistent with phosphorylation of TRAL by PNG relieving its ability to repress translation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the in vitro translation assay results with phosphomimetic and alanine-substituted TRAL.

claim: Threonine 644 of TRAL became phosphorylated at egg activation in wild-type but not png mutant eggs.
source: Nevertheless, we did observe that one of the threonine residues (T644) phosphorylated in vitro became phosphorylated at egg activation in wild-type but not png mutant eggs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phosphorylation levels of T35, S59, and S472 in TRAL were reduced in activated oocytes from png mutants.
source: Phosphorylation levels of several residues (T35, S59, S472) were reduced in the activated oocytes from the png mutant, although they were not found in the substrate screen.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: S214 phosphorylation in TRAL is increased in png mutant activated oocytes.
source: The proposal of phosphorylation downstream of PNG is consistent with two of these being in the N-terminus of TRAL that is not phosphorylated by PNG in vitro, and the observation that S214 phosphorylation is increased in png mutant activated oocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: TRAL phosphorylation is developmentally dynamic and involves several kinases.
source: Together these results support the conclusion that TRAL is a PNG substrate, but they reveal that TRAL phosphorylation is developmentally dynamic and involves several kinases.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the complex phosphorylation pattern of TRAL observed during egg activation.

claim: png mutant females produce eggs that complete meiosis but subsequently fail to initiate mitotic divisions.
source: The png gene was identified because mutant females produce eggs that complete meiosis but subsequently fail to initiate mitotic divisions (Shamanski and Orr-Weaver, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Shamanski and Orr-Weaver, 1991).

claim: DNA replication continues in png mutant embryos, resulting in embryos with giant, polyploid nuclei.
source: Nevertheless, DNA replication continues, resulting in embryos with giant, polyploid nuclei.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about png mutant phenotypes.

claim: In strong alleles of png there is no mitosis.
source: In strong alleles of png there is no mitosis, whereas weaker alleles permit a few mitotic divisions but these nuclei ultimately also become polyploid (Shamanski and Orr-Weaver, 1991; Lee et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Shamanski and Orr-Weaver, 1991; Lee et al., 2001).

claim: Weaker png alleles permit a few mitotic divisions but these nuclei ultimately also become polyploid.
source: In strong alleles of png there is no mitosis, whereas weaker alleles permit a few mitotic divisions but these nuclei ultimately also become polyploid (Shamanski and Orr-Weaver, 1991; Lee et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Shamanski and Orr-Weaver, 1991; Lee et al., 2001).

claim: The absence of mitosis in png mutants is due to a failure to promote cyclin B mRNA translation at egg activation.
source: The absence of mitosis in png mutants is due to a failure to promote cyclin B mRNA translation at egg activation (Vardy and Orr-Weaver, 2007; Kronja et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Vardy and Orr-Weaver, 2007; Kronja et al., 2014).

claim: Removal of one copy of pum can suppress the giant-nuclei png phenotype.
source: We demonstrated that removal of one copy of some genes (such as the translational repressor pum, discussed below) can suppress the giant-nuclei png phenotype, resulting in embryos that undergo more mitotic divisions and thus have more nuclei (Lee et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Lee et al., 2001).

claim: Removal of one copy of cyclin B enhances the png phenotype.
source: In contrast, removal of one copy of a gene such as cyclin B enhances the png phenotype, consistent with png having a positive effect on this gene (Lee et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Lee et al., 2001).

claim: Reducing the dosage of tral suppressed the png phenotype, permitting additional mitoses and increased numbers of nuclei.
source: Reducing the dosage of tral (a heterozygous tral1 mutation, which has a P element insertion) suppressed the png phenotype, permitting additional mitoses and increased numbers of nuclei (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Suppression of png by tral mutation was more pronounced with a deletion that completely removes the tral gene.
source: This suppression was even more pronounced with a deletion that completely removes the tral gene (heterozygous Df(3L)ED4483) (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cyclin B protein levels were increased in png transheterozygous embryos when the dosage of tral was reduced.
source: Strikingly, Cyclin B protein levels were increased in the png transheterozygous embryos when the dosage of tral was reduced (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The amount of Cyclin B was restored more with the tral deletion than with the tral1 allele.
source: Consistent with the suppression phenotypes, the amount of Cyclin B was restored more with the deletion than with the tral1 allele.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunoblot analysis.

claim: Cyclin A protein levels were increased in png mutants with reduced TRAL dosage.
source: Cyclin A, another PNG translational target, also was increased with reduced TRAL.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunoblot analysis.

claim: Phosphorylation of TRAL by PNG blocks its repressive effects on translation.
source: Taken together, the in vitro and in vivo phosphorylation results and the genetic interaction data indicate that phosphorylation of TRAL by PNG blocks its repressive effects on translation, permitting translation of cyclin B at egg activation to permit embryonic mitoses.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results including in vitro phosphorylation, genetic interactions, and protein level measurements.

claim: PNG phosphorylation of TRAL permits translation of cyclin B at egg activation to permit embryonic mitoses.
source: Taken together, the in vitro and in vivo phosphorylation results and the genetic interaction data indicate that phosphorylation of TRAL by PNG blocks its repressive effects on translation, permitting translation of cyclin B at egg activation to permit embryonic mitoses.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results including in vitro phosphorylation, genetic interactions, and protein level measurements.

claim: TRAL is present in large cytoplasmic RNP granules in mature oocytes in both Drosophila and C. elegans.
source: TRAL is present in large cytoplasmic RNP granules in mature oocytes in both Drosophila and C. elegans, and these disperse on egg activation (Weil et al., 2012; Noble et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Weil et al., 2012; Noble et al., 2008).

claim: TRAL RNP granules disperse on egg activation.
source: TRAL is present in large cytoplasmic RNP granules in mature oocytes in both Drosophila and C. elegans, and these disperse on egg activation (Weil et al., 2012; Noble et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Weil et al., 2012; Noble et al., 2008).

claim: TRAL granules became diminished by about 10 min after egg activation.
source: We found that early in activation, by about 10 min, TRAL granules became diminished (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In png mutant eggs, TRAL granules also disappeared with normal timing.
source: In png mutant eggs, the TRAL granules also disappeared with normal timing (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PNG does not appear to be involved in the reorganization of TRAL granules.
source: We conclude that PNG does not appear to be involved in this reorganization of TRAL granules.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that TRAL granules disperse normally in png mutant eggs.

claim: Dispersal of TRAL from granules occurs prior to when PNG becomes active at 30 min after egg activation.
source: Indeed, dispersal of TRAL from granules occurs prior to when PNG becomes active at 30 min after egg activation (Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the timing of TRAL granule dispersal and citation to published work (Hara et al., 2017) about PNG activation timing.

claim: PNG phosphorylation may directly affect the ability of TRAL to inhibit translation initiation.
source: PNG phosphorylation may more directly affect the ability of TRAL to inhibit translation initiation, as indicated by the effect of the phosphomimetic form on translation in reticulocyte lysates.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the in vitro translation assay results with phosphomimetic TRAL.

claim: pum dominantly suppresses png.
source: We previously showed that the translational repressor pumilio (pum) dominantly suppresses png; a heterozygous mutation of pum restores both Cyclin B protein levels and mitosis in png mutant embryos (Vardy and Orr-Weaver, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Vardy and Orr-Weaver, 2007).

claim: A heterozygous mutation of pum restores both Cyclin B protein levels and mitosis in png mutant embryos.
source: We previously showed that the translational repressor pumilio (pum) dominantly suppresses png; a heterozygous mutation of pum restores both Cyclin B protein levels and mitosis in png mutant embryos (Vardy and Orr-Weaver, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Vardy and Orr-Weaver, 2007).

claim: GST-PUM fusion protein is phosphorylated by purified wild-type PNG kinase but not by the kinase-dead form.
source: A GST-PUM fusion protein is phosphorylated by purified wild-type PNG kinase but not by the kinase-dead form (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ME31B RNA helicase acts as a translational repressor.
source: The ME31B RNA helicase acts as a translational repressor (Nakamura et al., 2001) and is a binding partner to TRAL (Tritschler et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Nakamura et al., 2001; Tritschler et al., 2008).

claim: ME31B is a binding partner to TRAL.
source: The ME31B RNA helicase acts as a translational repressor (Nakamura et al., 2001) and is a binding partner to TRAL (Tritschler et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Tritschler et al., 2008).

claim: PNG was able to phosphorylate ME31B in vitro.
source: Given its interaction with TRAL, we directly tested ME31B in vitro and found that PNG was able to phosphorylate it (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: BICC binds to the GNU subunit of the PNG complex directly through its SAM domain.
source: BICC binds to the GNU subunit of the PNG complex directly through its SAM domain (Chicoine et al., 2007) (Hara and Orr-Weaver unpublished), and BICC also is known to physically interact with TRAL (Kugler et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Chicoine et al., 2007) and unpublished data.

claim: BICC physically interacts with TRAL.
source: BICC binds to the GNU subunit of the PNG complex directly through its SAM domain (Chicoine et al., 2007) (Hara and Orr-Weaver unpublished), and BICC also is known to physically interact with TRAL (Kugler et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Kugler et al., 2009).

claim: PNG readily phosphorylates BICC in vitro.
source: Despite this, PNG readily phosphorylates BICC in vitro (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PNG may act on a number of translational repressors.
source: These results raise the possibility that PNG acts on a number of translational repressors.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that PNG phosphorylates multiple translational repressors.

claim: The two PNG substrate screens likely were not saturating to identify all potential translational repressor targets.
source: The two PNG substrate screens likely were not saturating to identify all potential translational repressor targets.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that some known repressors were not recovered in both screens.

claim: Cup and Caprin were recovered in the first substrate screen but not by the criteria in the second.
source: The translational repressors Cup and Caprin were recovered in the first substrate screen but not by our criteria in the second.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the substrate screens.

claim: PNG may inactivate multiple translational repressors by phosphorylation to promote translation of different sets of mRNAs at egg activation.
source: The dominant genetic suppression of png observed with mutation of tral or pum generates the hypothesis that PNG may inactivate multiple translational repressors by phosphorylation to promote translation of different sets of mRNAs at egg activation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from genetic interaction data and in vitro phosphorylation results.

claim: PNG's effect on multiple repressors may target a single set of mRNAs localized to RNP granules.
source: It is also possible that PNG's effect on multiple repressors may target a single set of mRNAs localized to RNP granules.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation that multiple PNG substrates are associated with RNP granules.

claim: BicC genetically interacts with tral.
source: BicC genetically interacts with tral, the protein appears to localize to the RNP granules in which TRAL and ME31B reside, and it binds to GNU (Kugler et al., 2009; Chicoine et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Kugler et al., 2009; Chicoine et al., 2007).

claim: BicC appears to localize to the RNP granules in which TRAL and ME31B reside.
source: BicC genetically interacts with tral, the protein appears to localize to the RNP granules in which TRAL and ME31B reside, and it binds to GNU (Kugler et al., 2009; Chicoine et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Kugler et al., 2009; Chicoine et al., 2007).

claim: PNG might phosphorylate multiple targets on RNP granules to de-repress translational inhibition of maternal mRNAs at egg activation.
source: From these observations, PNG might phosphorylate multiple targets on RNP granules to de-repress translational inhibition of maternal mRNAs at egg activation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that multiple PNG substrates are associated with RNP granules.

claim: PNG may indirectly affect translational repressors later in embryogenesis, at a developmental time when PNG appears to be inactivated.
source: In addition to its effects at egg activation, PNG may indirectly affect translational repressors later in embryogenesis, at a developmental time when PNG appears to be inactivated (Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on inference and citation to published work (Hara et al., 2017).

claim: TRAL, ME31B, and Cup proteins form an inhibitory complex that represses the translation of maternal mRNAs in the embryo.
source: In the embryo the TRAL, ME31B, and Cup proteins form an inhibitory complex that represses the translation of maternal mRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about translational repressor complexes.

claim: TRAL, ME31B, and Cup proteins are degraded during the maternal-to-zygotic transition.
source: These proteins have been shown to be degraded during the maternal-to-zygotic transition, and functional PNG is a prerequisite for this degradation (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Wang et al., 2017).

claim: Functional PNG is a prerequisite for the degradation of TRAL, ME31B, and Cup during the maternal-to-zygotic transition.
source: These proteins have been shown to be degraded during the maternal-to-zygotic transition, and functional PNG is a prerequisite for this degradation (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Wang et al., 2017).

claim: The PNG kinase is activated by a signal downstream of egg activation.
source: We previously showed that the PNG kinase is activated by a signal downstream of egg activation and thus controls massive changes in maternal mRNA translation (Kronja et al., 2014; Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Kronja et al., 2014; Hara et al., 2017).

claim: Phosphorylation by PNG suppressed TRAL's ability to repress mRNA translation.
source: We now have found TRAL is a PNG substrate using a biochemical screen. Phosphorylation by PNG suppressed TRAL's ability to repress mRNA translation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the biochemical screen and in vitro translation assays.

claim: Genetic interaction between png and tral in fertilized embryos suggests that TRAL phosphorylation by PNG during the oocyte-to-embryo transition is key to remodel maternal mRNAs' translation activity.
source: This antagonism also was supported by genetic interaction between png and tral in fertilized embryos, suggesting that TRAL phosphorylation by PNG during the oocyte-to-embryo transition is a key to remodel maternal mRNAs' translation activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from genetic interaction data and in vitro phosphorylation results.

claim: The PNG kinase functions as a signal transducer for the external egg activation signal to mRNA translation in the cytoplasm in activated eggs.
source: The PNG kinase functions as a signal transducer for the external egg activation signal to mRNA translation in the cytoplasm in the activated eggs (Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Hara et al., 2017).

claim: Similar strategies to PNG signaling can be used in oocyte maturation, during which a hormonal signal leads to phosphorylation of translational regulators to control mRNA translation.
source: Similar strategies can be used in oocyte maturation, during which a hormonal signal leads to phosphorylation of translational regulators to control mRNA translation (Radford et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Radford et al., 2008).

claim: In neurons, stimuli cause translocation of mRNA followed by translational activation.
source: In neurons, stimuli cause translocation of mRNA followed by translational activation (Yoon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Yoon et al., 2016).

claim: Understanding signaling pathways that transmit extracellular signals to translational controls is likely to provide insight into molecular mechanisms in fertility as well as synaptic plasticity and memory.
source: Understanding signaling pathways that transmit extracellular signals to translational controls thus is likely to provide us insight into molecular mechanisms in fertility as well as synaptic plasticity and memory.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the broader implications of the research findings.

claim: Peptides were robustly phosphorylated by the active PNG kinase complex in contrast to the kinase-dead control.
source: Peptides were robustly phosphorylated by the active PNG kinase complex in contrast to the kinase-dead control (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from positional scanning peptide library shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Peptides whose phospho-acceptor site was fixed with threonine were strongly phosphorylated by PNG.
source: PNG exhibited a strong preference to phosphorylate threonine, because peptides whose phospho-acceptor site (position 0) was fixed with threonine were strongly phosphorylated, whereas serine peptides were phosphorylated at reduced levels (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from positional scanning peptide library shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Serine peptides were phosphorylated at reduced levels by PNG compared to threonine peptides.
source: PNG exhibited a strong preference to phosphorylate threonine, because peptides whose phospho-acceptor site (position 0) was fixed with threonine were strongly phosphorylated, whereas serine peptides were phosphorylated at reduced levels (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from positional scanning peptide library shown in Figure 1A,B.
